questions.stem: The four stages of the software engineering project are:
options: Identifying and defining → designing → producing and implementing → testing and evaluating
Identifying and defining → research and planning → producing and implementing → testing and evaluating
Requirements → research and planning → producing and implementing → maintaining
Identifying and defining → research and planning → testing and evaluating → producing and implementing
questions.explanation: They are iterative — findings from testing feed back into earlier stages rather than ending the process. (D) reorders the last two, which is a tempting misreading of "test-driven".

questions.stem: SMART requirements stand for:
options: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Repeatable, Time-bound
Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound
Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Traceable
Structured, Modular, Automated, Robust, Testable
questions.explanation: (A) and (C) each change a single word to something that sounds like sensible engineering practice. The point of SMART is that a requirement written this way can actually be tested later — "the system should be fast" cannot.

questions.stem: The difference between functional and performance requirements is:
options: Functional requirements are testable; performance requirements are aspirational statements of intent
Functional describes how well the system must operate; performance describes what it must do
Functional requirements come from the client; performance requirements come from the developers
Functional describes what the system must do; performance describes how well it must do it
questions.explanation: "Users can book a room" is functional; "the booking confirms in under 2 seconds with 500 concurrent users" is performance. (A) has it backwards in spirit — a performance requirement written in SMART form is more precisely testable, not less.

questions.stem: A project boundary is:
options: The line separating what the system will do from what it will not, defining scope and expectations
The maximum budget and final deadline agreed with the client
A value sitting exactly on the edge of an accepted input range
The set of stakeholders whose approval is required before the project may proceed
questions.explanation: (C) is the deliberate collision: the same word means something quite different in testing, where a boundary value sits on the edge of an accepted range. Scope creep is what happens when the boundary was never written down.

questions.stem: Feasibility in a project context asks whether:
options: The project can realistically be completed within the available schedule and budget
The technology required exists and has been proven to work somewhere
The client has approved the design and signed off the requirements document
The finished solution will deliver a positive return on the money invested
questions.explanation: Schedule and budget are the two named dimensions; a feasibility answer that ignores both is incomplete. (D) is viability — a project can be entirely feasible and still not worth doing.

questions.stem: A stakeholder is:
options: The client who commissions and pays for the system, together with its end-users
Anyone affected by or with an interest in the system — client, end-users, developers, management, regulators
Any party whose formal approval is required before the system can be released
Any person who will interact with the system's interface once it is deployed
questions.explanation: Each distractor is a true subset, which is what makes them plausible — and what makes them wrong, since the omitted groups are exactly the ones that get forgotten. Missing a stakeholder is a classic cause of a solution that meets the specification but not the need: a validation failure.

questions.stem: A use case describes:
options: A written scenario used only to derive test data once the system has been built
The sequence of messages exchanged between objects while a single operation executes
How a user interacts with the system to achieve a goal — actor, trigger, main sequence and alternative/error paths
A structured list of the functional requirements the finished system must satisfy
questions.explanation: (B) is a sequence diagram — a different tool documenting internal behaviour rather than user goals. Use cases are used to derive functional requirements and to design test cases, which is why the error paths matter as much as the main sequence.

questions.stem: The four software implementation methods are:
options: Direct, phased, parallel, pilot
Waterfall, Agile, WAgile, Scrum
Unit, integration, system, acceptance
Direct, phased, parallel, incremental
questions.explanation: (D) changes one word to a term that genuinely exists elsewhere in software engineering. Do not confuse implementation methods (how you switch systems over) with development approaches (how you build) or test levels (what scope you test at) — all three sets appear as options here.

questions.stem: Direct implementation is characterised by:
options: Being low risk and high cost, because both systems run until the new one has proven itself
Being fast and cheap, but high risk, because there is no fallback if the new system fails
Being moderate risk, because problems surface at one site before the full rollout
Being low risk but slow, because the system is introduced one module at a time
questions.explanation: Old system off, new system on, at a set moment — defensible only where the consequence of failure is low. (A), (C) and (D) describe parallel, pilot and phased respectively, so all four methods appear as options.

questions.stem: Parallel implementation is the safest because:
options: Each module is proven before the next is introduced, limiting the scope of any fault
Only one site uses the new system at first, so any failure is contained to that site
The old system remains available as a fallback and the two systems' outputs can be cross-checked
The changeover happens at a planned moment, so staff can be fully trained beforehand
questions.explanation: The cross-check is the part students forget — parallel running does not just give you a fallback, it gives you a way to detect that the new system is wrong. Its cost is that it is expensive and doubles the workload during the transition.

questions.stem: A payroll system handling irreplaceable financial data should use which implementation method?
options: Pilot
Direct
Parallel
Phased
questions.explanation: Parallel — The choice depends on the consequence of failure, not on cost. Safety-critical or irreplaceable data → parallel; a low-stakes internal tool on a tight budget → direct. Say which factor drove your choice, or the justification earns nothing.

questions.stem: Pilot implementation means:
options: Introducing the system one module at a time across the whole organisation
Trialling the complete system with one group or site before the full rollout
Running the old and the new system side by side at every site
Switching the entire organisation over at a single planned moment
questions.explanation: The distinction from phased (A) is what is being limited: pilot limits who, phased limits how much. Issues are found and fixed at limited scale, and pilot users often become advocates during the wider rollout.

questions.stem: Phased implementation trades:
options: Faster delivery, in exchange for more intensive user training up front
Lower cost, in exchange for higher risk during the changeover period
Lower risk, in exchange for slower delivery and the complexity of managing the transition
Higher confidence, in exchange for running two systems at double the workload
questions.explanation: (D) is the cost of parallel implementation. During a phased transition, temporary interfaces between the old and new modules must be built and maintained — work that is thrown away at the end, and which students routinely forget to cost.

questions.stem: Waterfall is most appropriate when:
options: The team is new to the domain and expects to learn a great deal as it builds
Requirements are expected to evolve as users see working software
The client wants a demonstrable increment every two weeks
Requirements are stable and fully known, and thorough documentation is required
questions.explanation: Its strengths are clear structure, milestones and documentation; its weakness is that change is expensive and problems found late are costly to fix. (A), (B) and (C) are the three standard arguments for Agile.

questions.stem: Agile delivers value through:
options: A fixed scope and price agreed in full before development begins
A single release at the end, following extensive up-front documentation
Short sprints producing working software, with continuous user involvement
Formal sign-off at each phase gate before the next phase may start
questions.explanation: The trade-off is that final cost and scope are harder to predict, which is why fixed-price contracts — option (A) — sit so awkwardly with Agile.

questions.stem: WAgile is:
options: A form of Waterfall in which the testing phase is repeated after every release
An Agile variant replacing sprints with a continuous flow board governed by WIP limits
A hybrid applying Waterfall's structured up-front planning with Agile iteration inside each phase
A management framework for coordinating several Agile teams working on one product
questions.explanation: (B) is Kanban. WAgile is useful where an organisation needs up-front approval and documentation — for funding or compliance reasons — but wants iterative delivery within each phase.

questions.stem: Scrum and Kanban differ because Scrum:
options: Is an Agile framework, whereas Kanban is incompatible with Agile
Uses a continuous board governed by work-in-progress limits
Has no scheduled ceremonies, whereas Kanban requires a daily stand-up
Uses fixed-length sprints, with planning, review and retrospective ceremonies
questions.explanation: (B) is Kanban — continuous flow across a to do / in progress / done board, limited by WIP rather than by sprint boundaries. Both are Agile, which disposes of (A).

questions.stem: A sprint is typically:
options: Whatever length the items in the current backlog happen to require
1–4 days, producing a single demonstrable feature
1–3 months, producing a full release candidate
1–4 weeks, producing a potentially shippable increment
questions.explanation: (A) is the conceptual trap — a sprint's length is fixed in advance and the scope is adjusted to fit it, not the other way round. Each sprint is bracketed by planning at the start and a review plus retrospective at the end.

questions.stem: The product backlog differs from the sprint backlog because the product backlog:
options: Holds everything not yet built, from which a slice is pulled into the current sprint
Holds the current sprint's committed work, from which completed items are promoted upward
Holds completed work, whereas the sprint backlog holds work currently in progress
Is fixed once agreed, whereas the sprint backlog is reprioritised at the start of each sprint
questions.explanation: (D) inverts the stability of the two: the product backlog is continually reordered as priorities change, while the sprint backlog is deliberately protected from change once the sprint has begun. In Kanban the nearest equivalent is the 'to do' column, governed by WIP limits.

questions.stem: On a Gantt chart, dependencies are shown by:
options: The colour assigned to each task bar
The vertical order in which tasks are listed down the left
Links drawn between task bars
The horizontal position at which each bar begins
questions.explanation: (D) is the close one: a dependent task's bar does start later, but a start date is a consequence, not a notation — without an explicit link the chart cannot show why it starts there, or what happens if the predecessor slips.

questions.stem: The critical path is:
options: The single longest task in the project, which sets the minimum schedule
The sequence of tasks that consumes the largest share of the project budget
The sequence of dependent tasks that determines the shortest possible project duration
The tasks that have the greatest amount of float available to them
questions.explanation: A delay to a critical-path task delays the whole project. (A) and (D) are the instructive wrong answers: criticality comes from the chain of dependencies, not from any one task's length, and critical-path tasks have zero float by definition.

questions.stem: Float (slack) in a schedule is:
options: The spare time a non-critical task has before it would begin delaying the project
The contingency amount deliberately held back from the project budget
The gap left between the end of one sprint and the start of the next
The difference between a completed task's estimated and actual duration
questions.explanation: Float is time, not money — (B) is budget contingency, which is the same idea applied to a different resource. Consuming all of a task's float promotes it onto the critical path.

questions.stem: In a Learner Hours PWA build, "build database schema → front-end integration" is on the critical path because:
options: The front end has nothing to connect to until the schema exists — the dependency is genuine
Both tasks are estimated to take longer than any others in the project
Both are assigned to the same developer, who cannot work on them simultaneously
Both must be complete before the client's agreed review milestone
questions.explanation: Criticality comes from dependency, not from cost, duration or deadline alone. (C) is the sophisticated distractor — a shared resource does force sequencing, but that is a resource constraint, which can be resolved by assigning someone else; a genuine technical dependency cannot.

questions.stem: Which set names collaboration tools for project work?
options: UglifyJS, PurgeCSS and PostCSS
Jinja2, SQLAlchemy and Flask
Trello, shared documents and GitHub
Wireshark, Burp Suite and OWASP ZAP
questions.explanation: Shared platforms for communication, file sharing and task tracking — with version control platforms serving as both a technical tool and as evidence of process for the portfolio. The other three sets are back-end frameworks, front-end build tools and security testing tools.

questions.stem: Quality assurance in a project requires:
options: Recording every defect found, its severity, and the commit that resolved it
Running the full test suite at the end of each phase before that phase is signed off
Appointing an independent reviewer who took no part in building the system
Defining measurable quality criteria, checking continually against requirements, and addressing compliance and legislative obligations
questions.explanation: All four describe real quality activities, but (A), (B) and (C) are each a single practice — QA is the continuous framework they sit inside. "Must load in under 2 seconds" and "must pass all specified test cases" are the kind of measurable criteria set early.

questions.stem: The three named communication issues in project work are:
options: Planning, scheduling and tracking progress
Involving and empowering the client, enabling feedback, and documenting decisions
Involving and empowering the client, enabling feedback, and negotiating
Verification, validation and evaluation
questions.explanation: (B) substitutes one plausible practice for another. Feedback must be structured so that it is both given and acted on — a review nobody responds to is theatre.

questions.stem: Balancing what a client wants against technical feasibility and ethical considerations is which named issue?
options: A feasibility issue, since the constraint is technical rather than interpersonal
A communication issue, since the disagreement arises from unclear expectations
A quality assurance issue, since the requirement cannot be measurably satisfied
Responding appropriately to stakeholders — a social and ethical issue in project work
questions.explanation: The ethical element is what places it here rather than under communication — telling a client that what they want is achievable but wrong is not a communication problem. It sits alongside working individually versus collaboratively, which raises division of labour, shared credit and dependency risk.

questions.stem: Outsourcing appears in this module as:
options: A named social and ethical issue, concerning where a project's work is performed
A development approach, alongside Waterfall, Agile and WAgile
An implementation method, alongside direct, phased, parallel and pilot
A named strategy for responding to development difficulties — bringing in outside expertise for a specific problem
questions.explanation: The other named strategies are searching online for a solution and collaborating with peers. (A) is a real debate in industry, but it is not how the syllabus categorises the term here.

questions.stem: A Level 0 DFD (context diagram) shows:
options: Every sub-process within the system, together with its data stores
The whole system as a single process, with its external entities and data flows
The system's external entities and their relationships, with no processes shown
The whole system as a single process, with its data stores but not its external entities
questions.explanation: (D) is the sharpest trap — a context diagram deliberately shows no data stores at all, because everything internal is hidden inside the one process. A Level 1 DFD explodes that process into sub-processes and introduces the data stores.

questions.stem: Balancing a DFD means:
options: Each level contains roughly the same number of processes as the level above
Each level preserves the total inputs and outputs of the level above it
Every process shown has at least one input and at least one output
Every data store is written to by one process and read by at least one other
questions.explanation: Level 1 adds internal detail only — it never invents a new external input or output. (C) is the rule that excludes black holes and miracles, and (D) is another genuine DFD consistency check; both are real, neither is balancing.

questions.stem: A black hole in a DFD is:
options: A process with inputs but no outputs
A process with outputs but no inputs
A data store that is written to but never read from
An external entity connected directly to another external entity
questions.explanation: (B) is its mirror image, the miracle (or grey hole) — output produced from nothing. (C) and (D) are also genuine DFD errors, which is what makes this a four-way discrimination rather than a definition recall.

questions.stem: A DFD shows:
options: The decision logic determining which process runs next
The order in which the system's processes are executed
How data moves between processes, data stores and external entities
The structure of the tables in which the system's data is stored
questions.explanation: DFDs show where data goes, not when. Sequence (B) and decision logic (A) belong on a flowchart; data structure (D) belongs in the data dictionary or an ER diagram.

questions.stem: In a structure chart, a filled circle on an arrow indicates:
options: A conditional call
A data item
A repeated call
A control flag
questions.explanation: A control flag — (B) is a hollow circle — the two notations differ only by fill, which is exactly the kind of detail an exam tests. Rectangles are modules, lines show calls, and a curved arrow around a call shows repetition (C) while a diamond shows selection (A).

questions.stem: A class diagram represents each class as a rectangle divided into:
options: Name / attributes / methods
Name / methods / attributes
Name / inputs / outputs
Attributes / methods / relationships
questions.explanation: (B) differs only in the order of the lower two compartments, and the order is fixed — data above behaviour. Inheritance is shown with a hollow triangle arrow pointing from the subclass to the parent.

questions.stem: A storyboard communicates:
options: The sequence in which the system's internal modules call one another
The structure of and relationships between the system's stored data
A sequential visual representation of the user's interaction and the screens involved
The order in which the project's tasks must be completed
questions.explanation: It exposes missing steps in the user journey before any code is written, and communicates the intended experience to non-technical stakeholders. (A) is a sequence diagram and (D) is a Gantt chart.

questions.stem: A data dictionary documents each data item's:
options: Screens on which it is displayed and the fields where it may be edited
Relationships to other entities, including cardinality
Name, data type, size or format, validation rules and purpose
Access permissions governing who may read or modify it
questions.explanation: (B) belongs on an ER diagram. It is technical documentation that a future maintainer depends on, since the maintainer is rarely the original author — and the validation rules entry is what later drives test case design.

questions.stem: Pseudocode is best described as:
options: Source code with the executable lines commented out for later reinstatement
An algorithm description in English-like statements with defined structural rules and keywords
A written narrative of the algorithm with no fixed structure or reserved words
Code written in a simplified language that a specialised interpreter can execute
questions.explanation: (C) is the misconception worth killing: pseudocode is not free prose — NESA's version has specific keywords and indentation rules, and answers written as loose English lose marks. It lets logic be reviewed independently of language syntax, and the 2025 paper asked candidates to convert pseudocode to Python.

questions.stem: The back end contributes to a project through all of the following except:
options: Selecting technology appropriate to the problem
Robust error handling so that the system fails gracefully
Choosing the colour palette and type scale used across the interface
A well-designed API and data contract for the front end to build against
questions.explanation: Security engineering is the fourth named contribution — building security into the back end protects the whole system, since a front end cannot enforce what the server does not check.

questions.stem: Computational thinking in a project involves:
options: Analysing requirements, modelling the system, coding and evaluating the result
Decomposing the problem, writing pseudocode, coding the solution and testing it
Abstraction, pattern recognition, decomposition and debugging
Organising data logically, decomposing problems, interpreting patterns, and designing and implementing algorithms
questions.explanation: (C) is the closest — three of its four terms are genuine computational thinking components, but debugging is a development activity that has been substituted for algorithm design. (A) and (B) describe the development process, not the thinking method. Computational thinking is what makes a problem implementable by a human, machine or computer.

questions.stem: Programmed data backup in a project means:
options: Manually exporting the database at the end of each working week
Committing the project's source files to a remote repository on a fixed schedule
Configuring a cloud storage service to synchronise a folder automatically
Code-based routines within the solution that regularly copy data to a secondary location, supporting business continuity
questions.explanation: The word doing the work is programmed — (B) and (C) are automated, but the automation lives outside the solution, and neither protects the application's data. In the exam-safe Python subset, os and datetime with with open(...) are enough to demonstrate it.

questions.stem: Using with open("data.txt", "r") as file: is preferred because:
options: It allows the file to be read from and written to at the same time
The whole file is loaded into memory in one operation, which is faster
It acquires a lock preventing other processes from writing to the file
The file is closed automatically even if an exception is raised inside the block
questions.explanation: The guarantee holds on the error path, which is the case a manual file.close() reliably misses. Modes: "r" read, "w" overwrite, "a" append — using "w" where "a" was intended silently destroys the existing file.

questions.stem: Code optimisation means:
options: Modifying code or redesigning algorithms to improve execution speed, reduce memory use and enhance performance
Removing comments and whitespace so the source file occupies less space
Restructuring code into smaller, clearer functions without changing what it does
Replacing long variable names with shorter ones so less memory is required
questions.explanation: (C) is refactoring — the sharpest trap, because both improve the code but only optimisation targets runtime behaviour. (B) is minification, which applies to delivered web assets rather than server-side source.

questions.stem: Naming conventions matter because:
options: Shorter, consistent names reduce the source file's size and therefore its load time
The interpreter resolves consistently named identifiers more quickly at runtime
They are enforced by the language, so an inconsistent name raises a syntax error
Consistent, meaningful identifiers make code readable and maintainable — a requirement, not a stylistic preference
questions.explanation: 2025 marker feedback penalised unclear structure and overly complex nested control structures where a simpler one would work — naming sits in the same category of "the marker has to be able to read it".

questions.stem: A stub is:
options: A placeholder with the correct name, parameters and return type but no real logic
Temporary code that calls the module under test so that it can be exercised
A function that has been written but is not yet called anywhere in the program
A commented-out function kept in the file for reference during development
questions.explanation: (B) is its complement, a driver. Remember it as direction: a stub is called by the code under test; a driver calls it. Both let unit and integration testing begin before every component exists, and the 2025 paper gave a function stub as stimulus.

questions.stem: A driver in testing:
options: Stands in for a module that the code under test needs to call
Calls the module under test so it can be exercised before the rest of the system exists
Manages the connection between the application and its database
Orchestrates the stages of a continuous integration pipeline
questions.explanation: (A) is the stub. (C) and (D) are the everyday meanings of "driver" in adjacent contexts, which is why the term needs pinning down precisely.

questions.stem: Prototyping in a project is used to:
options: Build partial working versions to test ideas and gather feedback before full implementation
Build one module completely, to establish the standard the rest will follow
Produce a non-functional visual mock-up for the client to approve
Release an early build to a limited group of real users in order to find defects
questions.explanation: (C) is a mock-up — it looks right but does nothing, so it cannot test whether an idea works. (D) is closer to pilot implementation, which happens after the system is built rather than before. Users react far more usefully to something concrete than to an abstract requirements question.

questions.stem: User documentation differs from technical documentation because user documentation:
options: Records the design decisions taken, so users understand the system's limits
Explains how to operate the system — guides, help text and tutorials
Lists the agreed requirements, so users can confirm each one was met
Describes how the system works internally, in language a non-specialist can follow
questions.explanation: (D) is the elegant trap — audience alone does not decide the category; purpose does, and explaining internals is technical documentation however plainly it is written. Technical documentation is the data dictionary, diagrams, code comments and API contracts, and it exists because the maintainer is rarely the original author.

questions.stem: Implementing version control in a project supports:
options: Automatic detection of defects introduced by a particular commit
Tracking changes, collaboration and rollback — and provides evidence of process for the portfolio
Encryption of the source code held in the remote repository
Recovery of the working directory after hardware failure, removing the need for backups
questions.explanation: Rollback is what makes experimentation safe; the audit trail is what makes the process assessable. (D) is the seductive one — a remote repo is an off-site copy of your source, but it holds no user data and no environment, so it is not a backup strategy.

questions.stem: Verification asks:
options: Does the system comply with the legislation that applies to it?
Are we building the right system — does it meet the actual need?
Is the system usable by the people who will operate it?
Are we building the system right — does it match the specification?
questions.explanation: (B) is validation. A system can pass verification and fail validation — it does exactly what the spec said, and the spec was wrong. Mnemonic: verification checks the build against the document; validation checks the document against reality.

questions.stem: Black box testing means:
options: Checking outputs against expected results for given inputs, without examining the code
Designing tests to exercise every internal path and branch through the code
Testing carried out by someone other than the developer who wrote the code
Testing the assembled system against requirements rather than testing individual units
questions.explanation: (B) is white box. (C) and (D) are the interesting distractors because both are real distinctions on different axes — independence of tester, and level of testing — neither of which is what black/white box describes.

questions.stem: Path testing ensures that:
options: Every logical path through the code is executed at least once
Every function in the program is called at least once
Every value in the valid input range is submitted at least once
Every variable is assigned a value before it is read
questions.explanation: (B) is function coverage, a weaker guarantee — calling a function once leaves its else branch untested. Path testing is a white box technique: you cannot design the tests without seeing the code.

questions.stem: The three levels of testing, in order, are:
options: Unit → system → integration
System → integration → unit
Unit → integration → system
Integration → unit → system
questions.explanation: Unit tests one function in isolation, integration checks that unit-tested components work together, and system tests the whole assembled application against the requirements. The order runs from smallest scope outward.

questions.stem: The four categories of test data are:
options: Valid, invalid, boundary, random
Valid, invalid, boundary, extreme
Normal, abnormal, boundary, extreme
Unit, integration, system, acceptance
questions.explanation: (A) and (C) each swap in one plausible-sounding term. Testing one comfortably "normal" value does not score — specific, well-reasoned selection across all four categories does.

questions.stem: For a room booking system accepting times from 8:00am to 6:00pm, which are boundary values?
options: 7:59am and 6:01pm only
10:00am and 2:00pm
3:00am and 11:59pm
questions.explanation: Boundary testing covers values on the edge as well as just outside it — the classic off-by-one bug accepts 7:59am or rejects 8:00am, and only (A) would catch both. (C) is valid data, (D) is extreme.

questions.stem: Invalid test data is used to confirm that:
options: The system produces the correct result for a typical, expected input
The system does not crash when given a value far beyond the expected range
The system behaves correctly at the exact limits of the accepted range
Validation and error handling work — the input is rejected with a clear message
questions.explanation: The distractors are the other three categories: (B) extreme, (C) boundary, (A) valid. Note the standard is rejected with a clear message — silently discarding bad input is also a failure.

questions.stem: A test plan should document:
options: What will be tested, how it will be tested, and the expected result to compare the actual output against
Every test that has been run, with its outcome and the date it was executed
The defects found so far, ranked by severity, with a developer assigned to each
The features to be built, with the acceptance criteria the client has agreed to
questions.explanation: (B) is a test log, (C) a defect register, (D) acceptance criteria — three genuine project artefacts, none of them a plan. Recording the expected result before running the test is what makes a discrepancy meaningful.

questions.stem: A logic error is distinguished from a syntax error because a logic error:
options: Prevents the program from running at all
Runs without complaint and produces the wrong result
Causes the program to stop partway through execution
Is reported by the interpreter, with a line number
questions.explanation: (A) is a syntax error and (C) a runtime error. Logic errors are the hardest to find precisely because nothing reports them — which is also why the expected result column in a test plan matters so much.

questions.stem: Dividing by zero during execution produces:
options: A boundary error
A syntax error
A logic error
A runtime error
questions.explanation: Runtime error — the code is syntactically valid, so the interpreter accepts it, and the fault only appears when that line executes with that value. Opening a missing file is another example. (C) is tempting, but a logic error would run successfully and give a wrong answer.

questions.stem: Debugging differs from testing because debugging:
options: Is performed by the client, whereas testing is performed by the developer
Detects that a defect exists, whereas testing determines its cause
Locates and fixes the cause of a defect that has already been detected
Happens during development, whereas testing happens only once the code is complete
questions.explanation: Testing finds; debugging diagnoses and fixes — (B) is that relationship reversed. Techniques: read the error message and traceback, add print/log statements, use breakpoints and step through, isolate with a minimal test case.

questions.stem: Evaluating effectiveness requires:
options: Describing in detail what the finished system does and which features it provides
Comparing performance against the measurable criteria defined earlier, with evidence, and making a judgement
Reporting the proportion of test cases that passed and the defects still open
Collecting user satisfaction ratings and reporting the average score
questions.explanation: (C) and (D) are real evidence — but evidence is not evaluation until it is measured against a stated criterion and a judgement follows. Structure: state the criterion → state the evidence → make the judgement → note the limitation → recommend the improvement.

questions.stem: Feedback gathered during evaluation should be:
options: Reduced to a single satisfaction score so it can be tracked between releases
Recorded in full and retained as evidence that consultation took place
Collected from the development team, who understand the system's constraints best
Synthesised into a report, analysed, and incorporated into revisions
questions.explanation: Evaluation that never changes a decision is documentation, not evaluation — which is exactly what (B) describes.

questions.stem: A client's requirements are expected to evolve as they see the product. The best-justified approach is:
options: WAgile, because up-front planning fixes the scope before the client is able to change it
Waterfall, because its thorough documentation makes every change traceable
Agile, because short iterations with continuous client involvement absorb change cheaply
Waterfall with an extended requirements phase, so the evolution happens before development starts
questions.explanation: (D) is the elegant trap — it sounds like a reasonable adaptation, but you cannot front-load an evolution that is driven by seeing the product. Justify by naming the criterion (requirement stability) and saying why the alternative is worse: Waterfall makes late change expensive because everything downstream must be reworked.

questions.stem: A team chooses Agile, but the client is unavailable for feedback for the entire term. The likely outcome is:
options: The core benefit — continuously validated feedback — is lost, and the team iterates on its own assumptions
The team delivers faster, since sprint reviews no longer consume time
Documentation improves, since decisions must now be written down rather than discussed
The approach effectively becomes Waterfall, which is appropriate given that requirements are now fixed
questions.explanation: (D) is the sophisticated wrong answer: the process may drift toward Waterfall, but the team has none of Waterfall's compensating up-front analysis — so it gets the weaknesses of both. Approach selection must account for the client's capacity, not only the team's preference.

questions.stem: A hospital medication system passes every unit and integration test, but nurses report that it does not fit their workflow. This is:
options: A validation failure — the specification did not reflect the real need
A verification failure — the build did not match the specification
A performance failure — the system is correct but too slow for the ward's pace
An acceptance testing failure — the client signed off without trialling the system
questions.explanation: (D) is close and partly true, but it names the process gap rather than the failure type. Trace it back to identifying and defining: requirements were probably gathered from managers rather than from the nurses who would use it.

questions.stem: A project is two weeks late on a task that had three weeks of float. The correct response is:
options: Renegotiate the deadline, since the project has already slipped by two weeks
Recognise that the end date is not yet affected, but monitor closely — the task has consumed most of its slack
Move the task onto the critical path so that it receives priority attention
Add a developer to the task in order to recover the two weeks
questions.explanation: Float is precisely the amount of delay a non-critical task can absorb before it starts to matter. (C) misunderstands the critical path as a management decision rather than a property of the dependency network, and (D) adds coordination overhead to a task that is not yet hurting anything.

questions.stem: A client requests three extra features mid-project, with no change to deadline or budget. The best response is:
options: Absorb the additional work within the existing schedule, to preserve the client relationship
Assess and document the time and cost impact, present the options — extend, re-prioritise or defer — and get agreement in writing
Deliver the features by reducing the time allocated to testing and documentation
Add them to the product backlog and address them in a later release, without further discussion
questions.explanation: (D) wears Agile clothing but ducks the conversation — the client still believes they are getting three features. Making the trade-off visible keeps the decision where it belongs. Cutting testing to fit, as in (C), is how projects fail quietly.

questions.stem: A Gantt chart shows every task at 100% complete, but system testing has not begun. This most likely indicates:
options: The testing tasks carry float, so they are excluded from the reported completion figure
The project is finished, since testing follows delivery rather than forming part of it
The critical path was drawn too short, so the testing tasks fell outside it
Testing was never scheduled as work with a duration and an owner, or progress is being reported inaccurately
questions.explanation: (A) is invented but plausible-sounding — float affects scheduling flexibility, never whether a task appears in the completion figure. Testing and evaluation is a project stage, not something that happens after the work.

questions.stem: A student project must demonstrate management and documentation of development. The strongest evidence is:
options: A Gantt chart showing planned versus actual, a version control history, and a dated log of decisions with justifications
A detailed Gantt chart of the original plan, together with the finished, working program
The full source code with thorough comments and a complete data dictionary
A final report describing each stage of the project and its outcome
questions.explanation: Every option is genuine portfolio material; only (A) shows management. Planned versus actual on both time and scope is the core evidence of development that was managed rather than development that merely happened — a plan alone (B) shows only intention.

questions.stem: For a scenario with Student and ScholarshipStudent classes, the class diagram should show:
options: A hollow triangle arrow from ScholarshipStudent to Student
A hollow triangle arrow from Student to ScholarshipStudent
A filled diamond from Student to ScholarshipStudent
A dashed arrow from ScholarshipStudent to Student
questions.explanation: Inheritance arrows point from the subclass to the parent — the arrowhead marks the general case, which is why (B) is the most commonly drawn error. (C) is composition and (D) is a dependency. Markers reward correct standard notation explicitly.

questions.stem: Converting the pseudocode IF hours >= 120 THEN eligible = TRUE ELSE eligible = FALSE to Python, the most defensible version is:
options: eligible = hours >= 120
if hours => 120: eligible = True
if hours >= 120: eligible = true
IF hours >= 120: eligible = True
questions.explanation: Each distractor carries exactly one fault: (B) uses =>, which is not a Python operator; (C) uses lowercase true, and Python is case-sensitive; (D) keeps the pseudocode keyword IF. The boolean assignment in (A) is also simpler than an if/else that assigns True in one branch and False in the other — favour clarity.

questions.stem: Which Python fragment would fail in the exam editor?
options: from datetime import datetime
import pandas as pd
import random
import os
questions.explanation: The editor is locked down to the standard library — math, random, os and datetime. No pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib or scikit-learn, and no internet access, which is why questions on "programming an ML model" expect plain arithmetic and loops.

questions.stem: A candidate calls calculate_total() on line 3 and defines it on line 20. The result is:
options: A syntax error, reported before any line is executed
It runs correctly, because Python reads the whole file before executing any of it
A NameError at run time — the name is not yet bound when line 3 executes
A logic error, producing an incorrect result
questions.explanation: (B) is the widespread misconception, and it is half true — Python parses the whole file, which is why there is no syntax error, but the def on line 20 does not bind the name until execution reaches it. Calling a function before it is defined was explicitly named in 2025 marker feedback, alongside incorrect indentation.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest set of test data for a password field accepting 6–12 characters?
options: "secure99", "Passw0rd!" and "letmein22" — three realistic passwords a user might actually choose
"abcde", "abcdefghijklm" and "" — every kind of input the field is supposed to reject
"abcdef", "secure99" and "abcdefghijkl" — one at each end of the accepted range and one in the middle
"abcdef" and "abcdefghijkl" (boundaries), "abcde" and "abcdefghijklm" (just outside), "secure99" (valid), "" and a 5000-character string (extreme)
questions.explanation: (B) and (C) are each partial coverage — (B) omits valid and boundary-inside values entirely, and (C) never tests rejection. All four categories, with a documented expected result for each, is what scores.

questions.stem: A team must decide between building a payment module in-house and outsourcing it. The strongest justification structure is:
options: State the criteria — internal capability, timeline, security and compliance obligations, cost, long-term maintenance — assess both options against them, then say why the rejected option is worse
Compare the total cost of each option over three years and choose the cheaper
Describe the capabilities of each option in equal detail, then state a preference
Identify what comparable organisations do for payments and follow that precedent
questions.explanation: For payments specifically, PCI-DSS compliance is usually the deciding criterion — say so rather than leaving it implicit. (B) is the trap: a cost comparison is a real analysis, but it silently drops every other criterion that matters here.

questions.stem: A system meets every requirement, yet users make frequent errors. The appropriate response is:
options: Treat it as a design signal — usability test to find the cause, modify the design, then regression test
Accept the error rate, since the system satisfies every agreed requirement
Expand the training material and user documentation to cover the errors being made
Rewrite the requirements so they describe the behaviour users are actually producing
questions.explanation: (C) is the classic weak answer — training is what you reach for when you have decided not to change the design. "Modifying designs to improve functionality" is an explicit part of the testing and evaluating stage.

questions.stem: Which pairs a project stage with the correct artefact?
options: Testing and evaluating → the SMART requirements
Identifying and defining → the Gantt chart and critical path analysis
Producing and implementing → the feasibility study
Research and planning → DFDs, storyboards and the choice of development approach
questions.explanation: Requirements, feasibility, boundaries and stakeholders belong to identifying and defining; the Gantt chart and the modelling tools belong to research and planning. The SMART requirements are written in stage one and used in stage four — which is what makes (A) tempting.

questions.stem: A team writes the requirement "the app should be fast and easy to use". The best rewrite is:
options: "The app must load quickly and require the minimum number of steps to record a session."
"A logged-in user can record a driving session in under 30 seconds, and the dashboard loads in under 2 seconds on a 4G connection."
"The app must be optimised for speed and designed for ease of use on mobile devices."
"The app must be faster and simpler to use than the paper logbook it replaces."
questions.explanation: (D) is the most interesting distractor — it introduces a comparison, which feels measurable, but "faster than a paper logbook" has no number and no test procedure. Specific, measurable and time-bound, and therefore testable later, is the entire point of SMART.

questions.stem: Which risk most justifies parallel rather than direct implementation for a school's reporting system during report-writing period?
options: Teachers need less training, because the familiar old system stays available alongside the new one
Parallel is cheaper, since no single cutover event has to be planned and staffed
A failed cutover mid-period would leave teachers unable to complete legally required reports, with no fallback
The new system's interface differs from the old one, so staff would need time to adjust
questions.explanation: (A) is a genuine secondary benefit of parallel running, but it is not a risk and would not on its own justify doubling the workload. Consequence of failure, and its timing, drive the decision — the same system might justify direct implementation during the January holidays.

questions.stem: In a DFD for a booking system, an arrow drawn directly from the CUSTOMER external entity to the BOOKINGS data store is:
options: Correct, provided the data flow is labelled
An error — data must pass through a process
Acceptable at Level 1 but not at Level 0
Correct only if that data store is also read by at least one process
questions.explanation: Something must do the writing, and that something is a process. Along with black holes, miracles, unlabelled flows and store-to-store flows, this is one of the standard DFD errors markers look for.

questions.stem: The best reason to produce a storyboard before coding a PWA interface is:
options: It removes the need for later usability testing by confirming the flow in advance
It defines the screens precisely enough that the HTML structure can be generated from it
It records the agreed interface, so the client cannot later dispute what was delivered
It exposes missing steps in the user journey and communicates the experience to non-technical stakeholders while change is still cheap
questions.explanation: (C) is a real commercial benefit but a defensive one — it is about protecting the developer rather than improving the product. Change costs almost nothing on paper and a great deal after implementation: the same shift-left logic as secure design.

questions.stem: A project's evaluation reports only that "the client was happy". The weakness is:
options: Client satisfaction is subjective and so has no place in a technical evaluation
There is no measurement against pre-defined criteria and no evidence — satisfaction is one criterion among several
The client is not the end-user, so their view does not represent the people who use the system
Evaluation must be quantitative, and satisfaction cannot meaningfully be quantified
questions.explanation: (C) makes a real and useful point — but it would still be a weakness if the users were happy and nothing else was reported. Add functional coverage against requirements, performance measurements, test results, accessibility conformance and usability data.

questions.stem: Which is the correct relationship between unit, integration and system testing?
options: They are alternatives; a project selects whichever level suits its size and risk
They build on each other — units in isolation, then units together, then the whole assembled system against the requirements
Integration testing supersedes unit testing once the components have been combined
System testing is performed first, to establish which units require detailed testing
questions.explanation: Integration testing assumes the units already pass — which is precisely why stubs and drivers exist, so that testing can begin before every component is finished.

questions.stem: A developer fixes a defect and ships without re-running the earlier tests. The risk is:
options: The documentation will no longer describe the system's current behaviour
The fix may not compile, since the earlier tests would have caught a syntax error
A regression — the change may have broken previously working functionality, with nothing in place to detect it
The same defect may reappear, since its underlying cause was never recorded
questions.explanation: Re-running the existing suite after every change is what makes an automated test suite pay for itself — the cost is incurred once and the protection is permanent.

questions.stem: Which best demonstrates the justify verb applied to an implementation method?
options: "Parallel implementation is the safest of the four methods, because the old system remains available as a fallback and the outputs of the two systems can be cross-checked."
"Parallel implementation was used, which meant the old and new payroll systems ran simultaneously across two pay cycles while their outputs were reconciled against one another."

"Parallel implementation was used because the payroll data is irreplaceable and a failed cutover would prevent staff being paid; direct was rejected as it offers no fallback, and phased was rejected because payroll cannot be run half in each system."
"Parallel implementation costs more than direct and takes longer than pilot, but it carries the lowest risk of data loss during the changeover period."
questions.explanation: Decision, reasons, evidence, and explicit rejection of the alternatives — that last element is what "justify" specifically demands, and it is the only thing separating (C) from three otherwise well-written answers. (B) describes, (A) explains, (D) compares.

questions.stem: A team gathers requirements only from the school principal, not from the students who will use the system. The predictable outcome is:
options: A solution that meets the specification but not the need — a validation failure caused by omitting a stakeholder
A verification failure, since the built system will not match what was specified
A feasibility failure, since the principal cannot estimate the development effort involved
A quality assurance failure, since no measurable criteria will have been defined
questions.explanation: The system will pass verification perfectly — it does exactly what the (wrong) specification asked for. Stakeholders are anyone affected by the system, and requirements gathered from only one of them will be incomplete.

questions.stem: In Kanban, a WIP limit exists to:
options: Limit how many items are in progress at once, exposing bottlenecks and improving flow
Cap how many items may be added to the backlog within a given period
Set the maximum interval before the board must be formally reviewed
Restrict how many developers may work on a single item at the same time
questions.explanation: Kanban has no sprints — flow is continuous, and the WIP limit is the mechanism that replaces the sprint boundary as a constraint. When a column hits its limit, work stops and the team fixes the bottleneck, which is the whole point.

questions.stem: A structure chart shows module CalculateFee passing a value back to ProcessBooking. This is drawn as:
options: A labelled arrow indicating data returned upward
A labelled arrow with a filled circle at its tail
A hollow triangle arrow pointing to the calling module
A dashed line drawn between the two module rectangles
questions.explanation: Data passed down and results passed back up are both labelled arrows with a hollow circle. (B) would be a control flag, which signals a condition rather than returning a value — and a fee is data, not a flag.

questions.stem: The strongest argument for writing technical documentation during development rather than after it is:
options: Clients rely on the technical documentation to confirm that their requirements were met
Documentation produced during development is legally required for commercial software
Writing the documentation first forces the developer to design the component before coding it
Decisions and their rationale are still fresh, and maintenance — usually by someone other than the author — is the longest phase of the lifecycle
questions.explanation: Documentation written months later reconstructs what the code does but loses why it does it that way — and the "why" is what a maintainer actually needs. (A) confuses the audiences: clients read user documentation.

questions.stem: A project encounters an unfamiliar technical problem. The named strategies for responding are:
options: Searching online for a solution, extending the deadline, and reducing the scope
Searching online for a solution, collaborating with peers, and outsourcing for specific expertise
Prototyping the problem area, collaborating with peers, and outsourcing for specific expertise
Escalating to the client, extending the deadline, and removing the affected feature
questions.explanation: (C) swaps in prototyping, which is a real technique but belongs to producing and implementing rather than to this list. All three strategies should be recorded in the project log with the decision and its reasoning — that record is assessable evidence.

questions.stem: In an 8-mark question asking you to evaluate a developed solution, the weakest structure is:
options: Measured results compared against the original SMART requirements
Criteria → evidence → judgement → limitation → recommendation
A description of each feature the solution contains
A balanced discussion of strengths and weaknesses followed by a reasoned conclusion
questions.explanation: Description without judgement is the single most common way to lose marks on an extended-response question — and note the stem asks for the weakest, so three of the four options are good.

questions.stem: For a solution you developed, the most convincing evidence of quality assurance is:
options: Code review records showing that every commit was reviewed by a second developer
A complete test log showing every test that was run and its outcome
A defect register listing every issue found, its severity, and how it was resolved
Measurable criteria defined at the start, continual checking against requirements during development, and documented compliance with privacy and accessibility obligations
questions.explanation: (A), (B) and (C) are all real QA artefacts — but each is a record of one activity, whereas QA is the framework of criteria and continual checking they sit inside. Note that QA is continual checking, not a final inspection.

questions.stem: A team wants to reduce the risk that a late-discovered defect derails the project. The most effective structural change is:
options: Schedule a longer and more thorough testing phase at the end of the project
Test continuously from the start — unit tests alongside development, integration as components land — so defects surface while they are cheap
Move additional developers onto testing as the deadline approaches
Freeze the requirements early, so that no new defects can be introduced late in the build
questions.explanation: (A) is the intuitive answer and the wrong one — more testing at the end finds defects at their most expensive. (D) confuses requirement churn with defects; a frozen specification can still be implemented incorrectly. The same shift-left cost argument that drives secure development drives test scheduling.

questions.stem: The clearest sign that a requirement is not SMART is:
options: It describes how well the system must perform rather than what it must do
It does not name the specific user group to which it applies
It does not state a deadline by which it must be delivered
It cannot be objectively tested as either met or unmet
questions.explanation: (A) describes a performance requirement, which is entirely legitimate and is often the easiest kind to write in SMART form. Testability is the acid test: if you cannot design a test for it, you cannot evaluate the finished system against it.

questions.stem: A project's Level 1 DFD introduces a new external entity that does not appear at Level 0. This is:
options: Required by convention, since Level 0 shows only the primary external entity
Acceptable, provided the new entity and its data flows are clearly labelled
A miracle, since output is now being produced with no matching input
A balancing error — Level 1 may add internal detail only, never a new external input or output
questions.explanation: (C) is the close relative: a miracle is a process producing output from nothing, whereas this is a mismatch between levels. Balancing means each level preserves the total inputs and outputs of the level above.

questions.stem: Which statement about iterative development is most accurate?
options: Development proceeds sequentially, but any earlier stage may be revisited if a defect is found
Each stage is repeated until it has been completed to a defined standard before the next begins
The same functionality is written several times over, and the best version is selected
The project is divided into smaller parts developed incrementally, each iteration building on the previous one
questions.explanation: (A) is the sophisticated near-miss — that describes Waterfall with feedback loops, where the product still arrives in one piece at the end. Iteration is what allows feedback to change the product before it becomes too expensive to change.

questions.stem: A stimulus describes a small internal tool with a tight budget and a low consequence of failure. The best-matched implementation method is:
options: Pilot across six sites
Parallel
Direct
Phased over 18 months
questions.explanation: Direct — Right-sizing the method to the risk is the judgement being tested — the same reasoning that rules direct implementation out for payroll rules it in here. Over-engineering the changeover is a real cost, not a free safety margin.

questions.stem: When a question gives a scenario, the single most valuable thing you can do is:
options: Define each relevant technical term before applying it to the scenario
Reference the specific system, data or user group from the stimulus in every point you make
Cover every option the scenario could plausibly support, so that nothing is missed
Open with a summary of the scenario, to demonstrate that you have understood it
questions.explanation: Ignoring the stimulus is the single most-cited marker complaint across all four modules. (D) is the most common way to waste the first paragraph — the marker wrote the stimulus and does not need it repeated.

questions.stem: Which best distinguishes testing from evaluating?
options: Testing is carried out by the developer; evaluating is carried out by the client
Testing judges effectiveness against the criteria; evaluating establishes whether the system behaves correctly
Testing establishes whether the system behaves correctly; evaluating judges whether it is effective against the criteria and the original need
Testing occurs throughout development; evaluating occurs once, at handover
questions.explanation: Testing is largely a verification activity; evaluation is largely a validation and effectiveness judgement. (A) and (D) describe common tendencies rather than definitions — a client can test, and evaluation should happen more than once.

questions.stem: The most defensible way to demonstrate that a solution met its purpose is:
options: A walkthrough of the finished interface showing each feature in operation
Reporting each original SMART requirement against measured results — e.g. "dashboard loads in 1.4 s against a 2 s target; session logging completes in 22 s against a 30 s target"
A test report showing that every test case in the plan passed
Survey results showing users found the solution useful and easy to operate
questions.explanation: (C) proves the system does what you built it to do; only (B) proves it does what you promised. Closing the loop back to the requirements set at the start is what turns a description into an evaluation.

questions.stem: Across the whole project, the strongest evidence of professional practice is:
options: A working solution satisfying every functional and performance requirement in the specification
A complete set of modelling tools — DFDs, structure charts, class diagrams and storyboards — produced before implementation
Planned versus actual tracking, version control history, documented decisions with reasoning, criteria-based evaluation, and demonstrated response to feedback
A thorough test plan covering all four categories of test data, with a documented expected result for each
questions.explanation: Every option here is strong portfolio material, and (A), (B) and (D) would each earn marks — but each is evidence of one stage. Only (C) shows management across the whole project, which is exactly what SE-12-09 asks you to apply methods to manage and document, and it is assessable in a way that a finished artefact alone is not.

questions.stem: Which requirement is fully SMART?
options: "The dashboard shall render within 2 seconds for 95% of requests on a 4G connection, by the pilot release"
"The system should load quickly for most users"
"The system will use a modern front-end framework"
"Users will find the system easy to learn"
questions.explanation: Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound — and therefore testable later, which is the point of SMART.

questions.stem: The distinction between a functional and a performance requirement is that functional requirements state:
options: How well the system must operate
The acceptance criteria for sign-off
The technologies to be used
What the system must do
questions.explanation: "Users can cancel a booking" is functional; "cancellation confirms within 2 seconds under load" is performance.

questions.stem: A project boundary differs from a boundary value because the project boundary:
options: Is a value at the edge of a valid input range
Sets the maximum budget
Marks the deadline for delivery
Separates the system being built from everything outside it, defining scope
questions.explanation: The same word carries a different meaning in testing — the deliberate overlap is examinable.

questions.stem: Feasibility in this course is assessed against:
options: Technical novelty and market demand
Whether the client has approved the design
Whether the required technology exists anywhere
Whether the project can realistically be completed within the available schedule and budget
questions.explanation: Schedule and budget are the two named dimensions — an answer ignoring either is incomplete.

questions.stem: A use case documents:
options: The actor, trigger, main sequence and alternative or error paths for achieving a goal
The database schema for a feature
The tasks and their dependencies
The classes and their relationships
questions.explanation: The error paths matter as much as the main sequence — they become both requirements and test cases.

questions.stem: Missing a stakeholder most typically causes:
options: A verification failure at unit testing
A merge conflict during integration
A performance shortfall under load
A validation failure — the system matches its specification but not the real need
questions.explanation: It surfaces only when real users encounter the finished product, which is why it is expensive.

questions.stem: A Gantt chart's bar length encodes:
options: The task's importance
The number of people assigned
The task's duration
The percentage complete
questions.explanation: Duration — Percentage complete is usually shaded within the bar, and dependencies are shown by links between bars.

questions.stem: A task with two weeks of float is delayed three weeks. The project end date:
options: Is unaffected
Slips by two weeks
Slips by three weeks
Slips by one week, as the task is now critical
questions.explanation: Float absorbs delay only up to its length — the arithmetic is exactly what a stimulus question tests.

questions.stem: The critical path is best defined as:
options: The longest chain of dependent tasks, determining the minimum project duration
The most expensive sequence of tasks
The tasks with the highest risk rating
The tasks assigned to the most experienced staff
questions.explanation: Criticality comes from dependency and duration, not from cost, risk or seniority.

questions.stem: A collaboration tool's principal project benefit is:
options: A single source of truth with version history and a visible audit trail of decisions
Eliminating the need for status meetings
Automatic generation of the Gantt chart
Guaranteed data security for project files
questions.explanation: Named risks are tool sprawl, notification overload, access control and dependence on connectivity.

questions.stem: Which process diary entry best evidences EC-style ongoing evaluation?
options: "Login page complete. Usability check with two students showed the error message was missed; moved it inline beside the field and re-tested — both found it immediately."
"Completed the login page today."
"Spent four hours on the login page."
"Login page finished ahead of schedule."
questions.explanation: Activity, evaluation against a criterion, the resulting change, and re-verification — the full loop in one entry.

questions.stem: A budget omitting licence renewals and hosting will:
options: Understate lifetime cost and may lead to selecting the wrong option
Be rejected by the client automatically
Prevent the Gantt chart from being completed
Breach accounting standards
questions.explanation: Ongoing operating cost frequently dominates the comparison between a cheaper build and a cheaper run.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly matches an approach to a project characteristic?
options: Waterfall — requirements evolving weekly
Agile — a fixed-price regulated project requiring full up-front specification
Prototyping — requirements unclear and the interface is central
End-user development — a public-facing payments system
questions.explanation: (A) and (B) are each matched to the condition that most argues against them, and (D) applies a low-governance approach to a high-risk system.

questions.stem: WAgile is best described as:
options: A testing methodology combining black and white box techniques
An implementation method between phased and parallel
A hybrid applying Waterfall's structured planning with Agile iteration at defined points
A version control branching strategy
questions.explanation: It suits organisations needing up-front approval and documentation while wanting iterative delivery inside phases.

questions.stem: Scrum's fixed-length iteration is bracketed by:
options: A design review and a code freeze
A stand-up and a retrospective only
Sprint planning at the start, and a review plus retrospective at the end
A backlog grooming session and a release
questions.explanation: Kanban has none of these — it is continuous flow governed by WIP limits.

questions.stem: A Kanban WIP limit exists to:
options: Restrict how many items are in progress at once, exposing bottlenecks
Cap the project budget
Set the length of each iteration
Limit the number of developers on the team
questions.explanation: It replaces the sprint boundary as the mechanism that forces work to finish before more is started.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the product backlog from the sprint backlog?
options: The product backlog contains only the current iteration's committed work
The product backlog is fixed once agreed and cannot be reprioritised
The product backlog is maintained by the developers without client input
The product backlog holds all outstanding work, from which a slice is drawn for the sprint
questions.explanation: Reprioritisation is the point — a backlog that cannot change defeats the purpose of iterating.

questions.stem: A Level 0 DFD deliberately omits:
options: External entities
Data stores
Data flows
The system process
questions.explanation: Level 0 shows the whole system as one process with its external entities and net flows; data stores appear from Level 1.

questions.stem: Balancing between DFD levels means that:
options: Each process is decomposed to equal depth
Each level contains the same number of data stores
The external inputs and outputs crossing the boundary are identical at both levels
Processes are numbered consecutively
questions.explanation: A new external input at Level 1 means the scope changed — which must be resolved rather than drawn.

questions.stem: Which is a valid DFD connection?
options: Process → data store
External entity → data store
Data store → data store
External entity → external entity
questions.explanation: All movement of data passes through a process — the other three are the standard connection errors.

questions.stem: A DFD process labelled "Customer" rather than "Process Order" is incorrect because processes are named:
options: With the responsible department
With their level number only
With the data they consume
With a verb and object
questions.explanation: Nouns belong on data stores and external entities; a noun on a process usually signals a modelling error.

questions.stem: In a structure chart, an arrow with an open circle typically denotes:
options: A data item passed between modules
A control flag
A module boundary
An external entity
questions.explanation: A filled circle denotes a control flag — the two markers are distinguished by fill, which is easy to lose in a hand-drawn answer.

questions.stem: A class diagram's inheritance arrow points:
options: From the parent to the subclass, with a filled diamond
From the subclass to the parent, with a hollow triangle
Between any two classes, with a dashed line
From the subclass to the parent, with an open arrowhead
questions.explanation: Direction and head shape both matter — markers reward correct standard notation explicitly.

questions.stem: Which artefact best communicates a screen sequence to a non-technical client?
options: A Level 1 DFD
A structure chart
A storyboard
A class diagram
questions.explanation: It exposes missing steps in the journey while change still costs nothing, and needs no notation knowledge to read.

questions.stem: A data dictionary documents each field's:
options: Position on the user interface
Encryption algorithm and key length
Name, type, size or format, validation rules and purpose
Frequency of update
questions.explanation: It is technical documentation aimed at whoever maintains the system later.

questions.stem: Pseudocode's advantage over code for design review is that it:
options: Expresses logic in language-neutral form so reviewers assess the algorithm rather than syntax
Executes without a compiler
Automatically generates the implementation
Documents the database schema
questions.explanation: The 2025 paper asked candidates to convert pseudocode to Python — the two directions test different skills.

questions.stem: Which activity is design thinking rather than computational thinking?
options: Interviewing users and building empathy maps
Decomposing the system into modules
Designing an efficient sorting algorithm
Choosing an appropriate data structure
questions.explanation: Computational thinking makes it work, design thinking makes it usable, systems thinking makes it fit.

questions.stem: Recognising that a new rostering system will change payroll, leave management and reporting is:
options: Computational thinking
Systems thinking
Design thinking
Agile planning
questions.explanation: Interdependencies, feedback loops and unintended consequences are its named concerns.

questions.stem: Which activity is not a named contribution of back-end engineering to a project?
options: Appropriate technology selection
Robust error handling so the system fails gracefully
Wireframing the user journey
Security engineering protecting the whole system
questions.explanation: The fourth named contribution is interfacing with the front end through a well-designed API or data contract.

questions.stem: Quality assurance differs from testing because QA:
options: Occurs only at the end of the project
Defines measurable criteria and checks continually against requirements throughout development
Is performed exclusively by the client
Applies only to documentation
questions.explanation: Testing detects defects; QA is the surrounding process that keeps the work aligned to the requirements.

questions.stem: Which requirements tool is strongest for quantifying priorities across many stakeholders?
options: In-depth interviews
A presentation of research results
A prototype
A survey
questions.explanation: Interviews buy depth and context; surveys buy breadth and comparability. Using both is the strong answer.

questions.stem: A prototype's characteristic risk is that:
options: Users cannot provide meaningful feedback on incomplete software
It cannot be used for UI-heavy systems
Users mistake it for a finished product and fixate on visuals over function
It removes the need for requirements gathering
questions.explanation: Keeping early prototypes deliberately low fidelity is the standard mitigation.

questions.stem: Presenting research results to stakeholders is valuable primarily because it:
options: Surfaces disagreement early and secures decisions and funding
Demonstrates the amount of work completed
Replaces the need for written documentation
Shortens the requirements phase
questions.explanation: Its value lies in the disagreement it exposes rather than the approval it collects.

questions.stem: Direct implementation is characterised by:
options: Highest safety at highest cost
Fastest and cheapest, with no fallback if the new system fails
A staged rollout by module
A trial with one group before wider release
questions.explanation: The decision turns on consequence of failure, which is why it suits low-stakes internal tools.

questions.stem: Parallel implementation's defining benefit is:
options: The old system remains available as a fallback and outputs can be cross-checked
It requires no staff training
It completes the transition fastest
It limits risk to a single site
questions.explanation: (D) describes pilot — the four methods are distinguished by exactly this kind of detail.

questions.stem: A supermarket chain trials a new stock system in one store before national rollout. This is:
options: Direct
Phased
Parallel
Pilot
questions.explanation: Pilot — Its weakness is that the trial site may not represent the wider organisation.

questions.stem: Phased implementation's characteristic cost is:
options: Temporary interfaces between old and new modules over a long transition
Doubled data entry across the organisation
No fallback if the cutover fails
An unrepresentative trial population
questions.explanation: Risk is contained per module and training is spread, at the price of duration and interim complexity.

questions.stem: Which conversion method is most defensible for a payroll system?
options: Direct, to minimise cost
Parallel, given irreplaceable data and legal obligations
Pilot in one department
Phased over 12 months
questions.explanation: The cost of double entry is trivial relative to the consequence of staff not being paid correctly.

questions.stem: A stub is used in testing to:
options: Stand in for a module the code under test calls
Call the module under test from above
Generate randomised test inputs
Record test outcomes automatically
questions.explanation: A driver does (B) — the two are complements and are routinely swapped in answers.

questions.stem: Verification asks whether the team is:
options: Building the right system for the user's need
Building the system right against the specification
Building it within budget
Building it to an accessible standard
questions.explanation: Validation asks (A) — a system can pass verification and fail validation when the specification itself was wrong.

questions.stem: Which testing level assumes the components already pass in isolation?
options: Unit
Path
Black box
Integration
questions.explanation: Integration — It checks that modules and external systems exchange data correctly, which presupposes each works alone.

questions.stem: White box testing is distinguished by:
options: Designing tests to exercise specific internal paths, branches and loops
Checking outputs for given inputs without seeing the code
Testing performed by end users
Testing the system against the original requirements
questions.explanation: Path testing is a white box technique — you cannot design path coverage without seeing the code.

questions.stem: For a field accepting 1–100, which values are extreme rather than boundary?
options: "abc" and a blank entry
questions.explanation: Extreme data is far beyond the expected range and confirms the system does not crash; (C) is abnormal/invalid data.

questions.stem: Abnormal test data confirms that:
options: Typical operation is correct
Invalid input is rejected gracefully with a helpful message
Performance targets are met
